name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.
points.name: Gloo is the sector's tech platform

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.
points.name: AI and Faith convenes the ethics work

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
According to the Census Bureau's Business Time-Use Survey, 13.7% of firms in the Other Services category (NAICS 81, which includes religious organizations) reported using AI in the last two weeks as of the latest available period, up from 12.6% in the prior period. This represents the most reliable measure of AI adoption across the sector, though survey coverage of churches and faith organizations specifically remains incomplete. The sources make clear that religious institutions are at an early stage of AI deployment compared to other industries, with adoption growing but still far from universal.

Where vendors and money concentrate, the evidence points toward specialized platforms built for the faith sector. Gloo, which serves thousands of U.S. churches, offers AI models, developer tools, and infrastructure designed specifically for ministry workflows. Gloo's offerings include production environment tools, values-aligned AI models, and specialized agents for mission-specific tasks. The platform emphasizes alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing, reflecting the sector's distinct ethical concerns. Gloo Intelligence provides custom model design and deployment for organizations seeking to unify siloed data and enable data-informed decision making in ministry contexts, indicating that churches moving beyond basic adoption invest in tailored solutions rather than off-the-shelf enterprise software.

The ethical and values-based character of AI deployment in faith organizations distinguishes this sector's conversation from technology use elsewhere. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together to address control and power, privacy, bias, discrimination, and questions about human dignity as they relate to AI development and use. The organization's mission reflects that 85 percent of the world's population claims religious affiliation, and that religious traditions offer ancient wisdom relevant to AI governance. At the University of Notre Dame, the Institute for Ethics and the Common Good conducts multidisciplinary research on AI's impact on human formation and dignity in the AI transition, examining real-world challenges and developing applied solutions for ethical technology design and deployment in faith contexts.

The sources reveal a sector grappling with labor and dignity questions specific to religious work. According to researchers at Notre Dame, industry leaders discuss job displacement from AI in ways that sometimes treat faster and cheaper work as self-evidently beneficial, while some propose that freed time could support family, hobbies, and crafts rather than traditional employment. Faculty engaged in Notre Dame's DELTA project, which examines human formation in the age of AI, note that awareness of these issues is evolving in educational and faith settings. This tension between technological capability and religious values around work, vocation, and human purpose appears central to how faith organizations are approaching AI deployment decisions.

The Hartford Institute for Religion Research and Barna Group represent the closest approximations to sector-wide survey infrastructure, with Hartford maintaining a 45-year history of congregational research and Barna providing data on trends affecting faith, culture, and ministry. Pew Research Center's Religion and Public Life program periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces. However, none of the available source excerpts detail specific findings from these organizations on AI adoption rates, deployment patterns, or clergy perception of AI tools. Churches deciding whether to deploy AI encounter a landscape in which 13.7% of religious organizations report recent use, specialized platforms emphasize values alignment, and a robust ethics conversation has emerged, but reliable data on return on investment, risk profiles, and adoption drivers within the sector remains limited in these sources.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, convenes a multidisciplinary community to tackle pressing ethical issues. It promotes interdisciplinary research, policy leadership, and practical models for ethical AI design, development, and deployment. The institute will host a second DELTA summit focused on human formation and dignity in the AI transition. Sullivan notes that many industry workers “talk very flippantly” about job displacement and AI’s speed and cost, while Lily Abadal observes that AI awareness is evolving.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group, a Christian research organization, offers data and insights on faith, culture, and ministry trends. Their website hosts articles, reports, podcasts, courses, and services, including a free webcast replay that examines six trends shaping pastoral leadership. The site also promotes Barna’s latest research report, The State of Pastors, Volume 2, which explores how pastors navigate post-pandemic life and ministry across self-leadership, church leadership, and cultural leadership. A series of conversations features pastors Glenn Packiam, Rich Villodas, and Sharon Hodde Miller discussing leadership challenges and the health of the church. New Barna data indicates that one in three young adults is increasing church attendance, revealing who is leaning in and what they seek at church.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: Gloo AI offers faith-based and missional organizations a suite of trusted, values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks to help build AI that reflects their values. The platform provides an API-first system for inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, along with a connected infrastructure of production tools, trusted content, and models. Gloo AI reports the first comprehensive evaluation framework that measures AI alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing. It also supplies knowledge-graph integration, secure infrastructure, and specialized agents that coordinate workflows and power mission-specific solutions, with expert teams designing custom models and infrastructure for missional organizations.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith is an organization that brings religious and faith-based perspectives to discussions about artificial intelligence ethics. The group argues that emerging AI issues—including control, privacy, bias, discrimination, and questions about human identity—are fundamentally moral questions, and that the world's religious traditions contain "ancient wisdom" relevant to how AI should be developed and used. The organization works to connect theologians, tech creators, researchers, and ethicists to integrate faith-based values into conversations about AI's ethical implications, aiming to introduce "humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both."
